name: microbial-island-biogeography
title: Does the taxa-area relationship hold for microbes — and flatten?
question:
Does the taxa-area relationship — the microbial analogue of the species-area
law — hold under the MacArthur-Wilson equilibrium model when it is run in a
microbial regime, and is its slope z flatter than for macro-organisms?
hypothesis:
Microbial communities obey the same equilibrium logic as macro-organisms
(richness set by the crossing of area-driven extinction against isolation-
driven colonization), so a microbial regime should still give a positive
taxa-area slope (z > 0). But because microbes draw on an enormous taxa pool
(so islands rarely saturate), disperse widely, and turn over fast locally
(martiny2006microbial; hanson2012beyond), the area effect on extinction is
weaker and the measured slope should be *flatter* than the macro slope —
consistent with the observed microbial band z ~ 0.02-0.1 (hornerdevine2004taxa;
bell2005islands) versus the classic macro z ~ 0.15-0.35.
objective:
Reusing the MacArthur-Wilson equilibrium process (no new process), run two
regimes over the same log-spaced area gradient (isolation fixed): a MACRO
regime (n_pool=60, area_exponent=0.25) and a MICROBIAL regime (n_pool=300,
shallow area_exponent=0.10, high colonization+extinction). Measure the log-log
taxa-area slope z for each on a 6-seed ensemble mean, measure the gross
equilibrium turnover rate, and render the macro-vs-microbe overlay.
description:
Microbial island biogeography (martiny2006microbial; hanson2012beyond) revived
the MacArthur-Wilson framework for microbes and found that the classic laws
hold in sign but differ sharply in degree. Horner-Devine et al. (2004,
hornerdevine2004taxa) measured a shallow taxa-area slope z ~ 0.02-0.1 for salt-
marsh sediment bacteria; Bell et al. (2005, bell2005islands) found a positive
but low z for bacteria in water-filled tree holes. The flatness is attributed
to a vast species pool (islands never saturate it), high passive dispersal
(little colonization limitation), and rapid local turnover.
This study does not build a new model: it reuses the already-validated
mw_equilibrium process in a microbial parameter regime (the microbial_island
composite) and compares it, on the same area gradient, to the macro regime the
species-area-and-isolation study calibrated. The microbial regime's shallow
area-extinction exponent reproduces the observed flat taxa-area slope while the
high per-taxon rates reproduce the fast turnover. The Earth Microbiome Project
(global 16S taxa-area surveys) and the tree-hole bacterial datasets
(bell2005islands) are the natural empirical validation targets for the measured
z and turnover. Builds on species-area-and-isolation, which established that the
process sits on the equilibrium rate curves and gives z ~ 0.12 in the macro
regime.

expected_behavior.name: microbial-sar-holds
expected_behavior.en:
The microbial taxa-area relationship holds: equilibrium richness increases
with patch area as a power law with a clearly positive slope z.
expected_behavior.rationale:
Even with a large pool and fast turnover, larger patches carry larger per-
taxon populations and so lose taxa less often; the equilibrium S* still rises
with area, giving a positive taxa-area slope (martiny2006microbial).

expected_behavior.name: microbial-z-flatter
expected_behavior.en:
The microbial taxa-area slope is flatter than the macro slope (z_micro <
z_macro), matching the observed shallow microbial band z ~ 0.02-0.1.
expected_behavior.rationale:
A huge taxa pool keeps microbial islands far from saturation and high
dispersal weakens colonization limitation, so the area effect on richness is
weaker than for macro-organisms (hornerdevine2004taxa; bell2005islands).

behavior_tests.name: microbial-sar-holds
behavior_tests.description: Microbial log-log taxa-area slope z must be positive.

provenance.note:
Measured z_micro = 0.0429 (area gradient 1-100, isolation 0, 6-seed
ensemble; microbial regime n_pool=300, colonization_base=0.10,
extinction_base=0.06, area_exponent=0.10). Positive and squarely inside
the empirical microbial band z ~ 0.02-0.1 (hornerdevine2004taxa salt-
marsh sediment; bell2005islands tree-hole bacteria).

behavior_tests.name: microbial-z-flatter
behavior_tests.description: Microbial taxa-area slope must be flatter than the macro slope.

provenance.note:
Measured z_micro = 0.0429 vs z_macro = 0.1227 over the identical area
gradient and seeds (6-seed ensemble), so z_flatter_margin =
z_macro - z_micro = 0.0798 > 0. z_macro reproduces the 0.12 slope the
species-area-and-isolation study measured in the macro regime. The
microbial slope is ~2.9x flatter, consistent with the observed microbe-
vs-macro contrast (hornerdevine2004taxa; hanson2012beyond). Gross
equilibrium turnover is ~20x higher in the microbial regime (25.99 vs
1.27 events · gen⁻¹ · island⁻¹), the fast-turnover signature.

pipeline_gate.proceed_condition:
With the microbial taxa-area relationship shown to hold and flatten relative
to the macro regime, the equilibrium model is validated against the microbial
island-biogeography literature and is ready for empirical calibration against
the Earth Microbiome Project and tree-hole bacterial datasets.

conclusion:
The taxa-area relationship holds for microbes and is markedly flatter than for
macro-organisms. Over an identical area gradient (6-seed ensemble), the
microbial regime gives a positive slope z_micro = 0.043 — inside the observed
microbial band z ~ 0.02-0.1 (Horner-Devine 2004; Bell 2005) — against a macro
slope z_macro = 0.123, a ~2.9x flattening. Gross equilibrium turnover is ~20x
higher in the microbial regime (25.99 vs 1.27 events per island per
generation), the fast-turnover signature a large pool and high dispersal
predict (Martiny 2006; Hanson 2012). The same equilibrium mechanism therefore
reproduces both the microbial and macro regimes with no new process; the Earth
Microbiome Project and tree-hole bacterial surveys are the next calibration
targets.

findings.statement: The taxa-area relationship holds for microbes but is flatter (z ~ 0.04 vs macro 0.12, ~3x) with ~20x faster turnover, consistent with the empirical microbial taxa-area literature (Horner-Devine 2004; Bell 2005).
